title: Russian Missiles Fall in Poland as COP31 Overruns and APEC Wraps Up
shortdescription: Missiles land in southeast Poland during a Russian attack on Ukraine, COP31 talks run past their deadline in Antalya, and APEC leaders issue a declaration in Shenzhen.

sub.title: Security fears, climate talks and trade diplomacy collide
sub.descr: It has been a tense few days on the world stage. A Russian attack on Ukraine sent missiles into NATO member Poland, the UN climate summit in Turkey ran past its deadline with countries still arguing over fossil fuels and money, and Asia-Pacific leaders wrapped up their summit in China with a joint declaration. Each story is different, but they share one theme: whether countries can still agree on rules when trust is low. Here is a plain-English guide to the biggest international stories right now.

sub.title: Russian Missiles Land in Southeast Poland
sub.descr: During Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine on November 20, two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory in the southeast, according to Poland's Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz. They came down near Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Molodycz, and one was reportedly a Kh-101 cruise missile. No injuries or damage were reported in Poland. In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said the same attack killed at least eight civilians and injured more than two dozen. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared Poland was "dealing with an intentional provocation." NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called it a "grave violation" of Polish airspace. President Donald Trump took a lighter line, describing it as "a couple of little missiles, by mistake." Analysts say it is unlikely NATO would invoke Article 5, its collective defence clause, over this incident, and that the more likely response is stronger air defence and closer coordination.

sub.title: COP31 Runs Into Overtime in Antalya
sub.descr: The UN climate summit was due to finish on Friday, November 20, but negotiators missed that deadline and kept working through Saturday and into the early hours of Sunday. COP31 President Murat Kurum told a late-night session, "We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon." The big sticking points are familiar: whether the final text should call for moving away from fossil fuels, and how much money richer countries will provide to help poorer ones adapt to climate impacts. An earlier draft was criticised for leaving out fossil fuels, and countries including France and Panama wanted a clear commitment on coal, oil and gas. Some decisions, including on cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, have already been adopted. At the time of writing, the full package had not been confirmed as approved, so check for the final outcome before publishing. This is also the first COP since the UN environmental body confirmed that global warming is set to pass 1.5°C.

sub.title: APEC Leaders Issue the Shenzhen Declaration
sub.descr: In China, leaders from all 21 APEC economies met in Shenzhen, with President Xi Jinping chairing the 33rd Economic Leaders' Meeting, and issued the 2026 APEC Leaders' Declaration on November 21. In it, they committed to "maintain macroeconomic stability, promote productivity and dynamism," and to advance regional economic integration in a market-driven way, including work towards the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific. The declaration focuses on four areas: trade and investment, connectivity, innovation and economic growth. Leaders also endorsed an APEC Trade Digitalization Cooperation Framework for 2027 to 2030, an APEC Connectivity Blueprint, and a statement on using digital and emerging technologies to support jobs. Viet Nam will host next year's meeting in Phu Quoc.

sub.title: What to Watch Next
sub.descr: There are three things to follow. First, whether COP31 delegates formally approve the final text, and whether it mentions fossil fuels or firm money for adaptation. Second, how NATO and Poland respond in the coming days, including any extra air defence for the eastern flank and whether Warsaw asks for formal consultations. Third, whether the broader push for peace in Ukraine continues after this latest attack. With so much moving at once, expect the headlines to keep changing, and check the latest updates before you publish.

title: Ukraine Peace Talks Stall as COP31 Opens in Antalya and APEC Looms in Shenzhen
shortdescription: Ukraine peace talks end without a breakthrough, COP31 opens in Turkey with the US absent, and Europe's economy faces new shocks as leaders prepare for the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

sub.title: A busy week for global diplomacy
sub.descr: If you've been trying to keep up with what's happening around the world, this week hasn't made it easy. In the space of a few days, US envoys have been shuttling between Abu Dhabi and Moscow in a push to end the war in Ukraine, world leaders have gathered in Turkey for the UN climate summit, and Europe's biggest economy has been hit by fresh warning signs. Meanwhile, Asia-Pacific leaders are getting ready to meet in China next week. Some of these stories are moving fast and others are playing out slowly, but they're all connected by one question: can countries still cooperate when tensions are this high? Here's a plain-English guide to the biggest international stories right now.

sub.title: Ukraine Peace Talks End Without a Breakthrough
sub.descr: Two days of talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a major breakthrough, though there was one concrete result. Ukrainian negotiator Rustem Umerov said both sides agreed to a large-scale prisoner exchange, which will bring relief to many families. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff then flew on to Moscow, arriving early on November 12, according to Russian state media. Kushner struck a hopeful but careful tone, saying, "We see some openings and some opportunities." Secretary of State Marco Rubio added that any security guarantees for Ukraine would also have to be acceptable to Russia, which is likely to be a sticking point. On the ground, the fighting hasn't paused. Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after the talks ended, and strikes on six major power substations caused outages across the country on November 11. A Russian attack on a crowded market in Odesa Oblast killed at least four people. Ukraine, for its part, has kept up drone attacks on Russian oil facilities, including the Omsk refinery, about 2,500 kilometres from the border.

sub.title: COP31 Opens in Antalya With the US Missing
sub.descr: The UN's annual climate summit, COP31, kicked off on Monday, November 9, in the Turkish resort city of Antalya and runs until November 20. About 68,500 people have registered, and negotiators from nearly 200 countries are taking part. Turkey is the official host, while Australia is leading the negotiations, a compromise after the two countries both wanted the job. One country is conspicuously missing. The United States has pulled out of climate negotiations again under President Trump. The mood is blunt. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said, "For too many people, climate change is deadly." Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the COP31 president, went further, saying, "This is the first COP where it is clear beyond a reasonable doubt that the world will overshoot the 1.5-degree target." The big fights are over money for poorer countries to adapt to climate impacts, a faster move away from fossil fuels and a plan to lift electricity's share of energy use from 21% to 35% by 2035. The war in Iran, which has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, has pushed up fuel and fertilizer prices and given renewable energy an extra push.

sub.title: Europe Faces Economic and Tech Shocks
sub.descr: Europe has plenty to worry about besides the war. In Dublin on November 11, European leaders met for the European Political Community summit with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in attendance. Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin said three of the EU's negotiating clusters with Ukraine have now opened, and he hopes to open the remaining two before Ireland's presidency ends. Back home, there's a more worrying business story. Mercedes-Benz has stopped new investment in its German plants and is considering closures, a sign of the pressure on Germany's car industry. On the tech side, a Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot for thousands of users, and the last day of Web Summit in Lisbon was dominated by talk of an AI bubble and fears of a financial crisis. Together, these stories show how fragile confidence is in both Europe's industrial base and the AI boom.

sub.title: What to Watch Next: APEC in Shenzhen and the Final Days of COP31
sub.descr: The next week is packed. China hosts the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19, under the motto "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." It's the third time China has hosted the event, and the city has already tightened rules on things like e-scooters ahead of the summit. Taiwan is expected to send a special representative on behalf of President Lai Ching-te. Back in Turkey, COP31 will head into its final days, and the question is whether countries can agree on clearer funding promises after the disappointing outcomes of COP29 and COP30. And of course, all eyes will stay on Moscow and Kyiv to see if the prisoner exchange leads to a bigger deal. With so much happening at once, expect the next few days to bring plenty of headlines.

title: UAE Reports New Iran Drone Attacks as Strait of Hormuz Crisis Worsens
shortdescription: UAE reports fresh Iran drone and missile attacks as the Strait of Hormuz crisis worsens, raising fears of wider conflict and oil disruption.

sub.title: UAE Says It Stopped Another Wave of Iranian Attacks
sub.descr: The UAE announced that its air defenses intercepted missile and drone strikes from Iran for the second day in a row. Officials there warned that the fragile truce between the US and Iran is now at serious risk of collapsing. The UAE called the attacks a major escalation and said it has every right to defend itself. Iran quickly denied being behind any recent missile or drone strikes on Emirati territory. A spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps argued that if Iran had actually carried out such attacks, Tehran would have publicly claimed responsibility. But in a warning directed at the UAE, an Iranian military spokeswoman said any attacks on Iran launched from Emirati soil would be met with a "crushing response." The latest violence follows a drone attack the day before that set fire to a major oil facility in Fujairah, injuring at least three people. Emirati authorities insist they shot down all incoming missiles, though they admitted some key energy infrastructure did suffer damage.

sub.title: Why You Should Be Paying Attention
sub.descr: Here's why this matters: the truce was never rock solid to begin with, and these strikes prove it. Even as diplomats keep talking publicly, the fighting around the Strait of Hormuz could easily spiral into a much larger regional war. And because so much of the world's oil passes through that narrow waterway, the fallout won't stay local. Expect shipping delays, higher fuel prices, and broader economic pain if things get worse.

sub.title: What's Happening in the Strait of Hormuz and 'Project Freedom'
sub.descr: All of this is unfolding while the US pushes ahead with something called 'Project Freedom' — a military mission designed to escort commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz. That waterway normally carries nearly a fifth of the world's oil and gas, but it's been largely shut down since the crisis exploded earlier this year. On Monday, US Marines said they destroyed six Iranian small boats along with incoming cruise missiles and drones targeting both Navy and commercial vessels. The US added that only two American-flagged ships have made it through the strait so far. Iran rejected that account entirely, accusing American forces of attacking civilian and cargo ships instead. Tehran has also threatened to pack the strait with mines, drones, missiles, and fast-attack boats — making commercial traffic incredibly dangerous. International organizations say the prolonged standoff has already left more than 800 ships and roughly 20,000 crew members trapped in the Gulf.

sub.title: US and Iranian Leaders Trade Warnings
sub.descr: Despite the fresh violence, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth insisted the ceasefire is still intact. He described Project Freedom as a temporary measure. 'We're not looking for a fight,' Hegseth said, though he added that the US would keep watching the situation closely. Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, accused Washington of breaking the ceasefire and warned that Iran hasn't 'even begun yet.' Secretary of State Marco Rubio said commercial crews are effectively being 'held hostage' in the strait, and stressed that the US won't let Iran treat attacks on shipping routes as normal. President Donald Trump, for his part, tried to downplay the latest clashes, calling them a 'little skirmish' and insisting that Iran still wants to strike a deal.

sub.title: Diplomacy Isn't Dead Yet
sub.descr: Fighting aside, diplomatic talks between the US and Iran are still happening, reportedly with Pakistan acting as a mediator. Iran has put forward a 14-point peace plan focused on lifting blockades and creating a new system to manage traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said negotiations are moving along, though he warned the US and UAE not to get stuck in a larger 'quagmire.' Pakistani officials involved in the talks say both sides have narrowed their differences on several issues, but no major breakthrough has been announced. The US and Iran held one direct round of talks in Islamabad last month, but follow-up meetings have stalled. Trump keeps demanding that Iran hand over its stockpiles of enriched uranium, while Tehran insists its nuclear program is purely peaceful.

sub.title: The Economic Toll and Global Pressure
sub.descr: The ongoing war is already rattling global energy markets. Oil prices are up, and shipping routes and fuel supplies remain under strain because the Strait of Hormuz is still so unstable. The UAE's Fujairah port — a major oil export hub that sends crude across the strait — has become even more critical during the crisis. Damage to facilities there has fueled fresh worries about supply disruptions. On the other side, the US naval blockade is squeezing Iran's economy by making it harder for the country to import goods and export oil. At the same time, rising fuel prices and sluggish economic growth are putting political pressure on Trump as congressional elections approach. Analysts say neither Washington nor Tehran seems willing to make major concessions right now — each side still believes it has leverage in this fight.

title: Belfast Riots Intensify After Alleged Assault Sparks Unrest
shortdescription: Belfast riots intensified after an alleged assault case sparked anti-immigration unrest, prompting a major police response across Northern Ireland.

sub.title: Violence Erupts in Belfast
sub.descr: Violence erupts in Belfast after protests over alleged assault by Sudanese asylum seeker turn into broader anti-immigration protests. Initial fears for public safety were soon replaced by wider immigration grievances, bringing larger numbers into different neighbourhoods. By nightfall tensions had escalated. Police cited incidents of thrown projectiles, fires and attacks on property. Local residents spoke of chaotic scenes with smoke from burning debris filling the streets. Authorities repeatedly reminded the public that the alleged assault is still under legal investigation and warned against spreading rumors that could inflame the situation. Police and officials urged calm while officers worked to regain control.

sub.title: Riots Cause Widespread Property Damage and Police Injuries
sub.descr: The unrest became one of the most serious episodes of public disorder Northern Ireland has seen in months. Rioters targeted vehicles, set fire to bins and structures and vandalised properties resulting in a heavy police presence. Emergency services were stretched responding to multiple incidents across the city at once. Several officers were injured and the Police Service of Northern Ireland condemned the attacks as unacceptable violence directed at both police and local communities. Residents reported seeing smashed windows, scorched streets and damaged vehicles. Authorities confirmed investigations were underway to identify those responsible. Officials stressed that peaceful protest is a democratic right but intimidation and violence would not be tolerated.

sub.title: Riot Revives Immigration Row
sub.descr: The violence has sparked the row over immigration and treatment of asylum seekers in the UK. Some protesters expressed concerns about border policy while community leaders warned that the protests had the potential to stir hostility towards immigrant populations not involved in the alleged assault. Human rights groups and advocacy organizations called for restraint. They urged residents not to target individuals based on their nationality or immigration status. The violence was condemned by political leaders across Northern Ireland who said the legal system must handle criminal probes independently. Several officials warned that tensions if allowed to fester could further widen cracks in already-fragile communities. The events highlighted how quickly a local flare-up can become intertwined with broader national discussions on immigration and public policy.

sub.title: Authorities Work to Restore Stability
sub.descr: Police and government officials were still working to restore stability to the city while also investigating both the alleged assault and the ensuing unrest. Security operations continued as officials tried to prevent further trouble and reassure residents. Leaders from across the political spectrum called for calm and urged residents to work through official channels rather than take to the streets to air their grievances. Authorities are reviewing video footage, eyewitness reports and other information to determine who committed crimes. Authorities promised to help local citizens and commerce affected by the riots, and community groups called for dialogue to help cool tempers. Belfast is slowly coming out of a string of nights of unrest, presenting a tough task for authorities. They need to keep public order as they tackle deep-seated issues that have added fuel to the fire in talks of immigration, community relations and public safety across Northern Ireland. Locals voiced relief, frustration and concern; a reminder of how fast underlying social tensions can come to the surface when local events are mixed with national discussions.

title: Germany Blames Russia for Explosive Drone Attack at Airport, Moves Against Moscow
shortdescription: Germany has accused Russia of being behind a failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport and announced diplomatic and security measures in response.

sub.title: Leipzig/Halle Airport Explosive Drone
sub.descr: The incident took place at Leipzig/Halle Airport, a major logistics hub in eastern Germany that plays an important role in European freight operations and support activities related to Ukraine. On Aug. 4, German authorities reported finding a drone loaded with explosives near a Ukrainian aircraft. Bomb disposal experts later made the device safe, preventing it from causing major damage. Officials said the attack was a serious escalation because it involved an attempted strike against critical transportation infrastructure. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that investigators believe, based on police findings, intelligence information and analysis of the attack pattern, that Russia was responsible.

sub.title: Berlin Links Assault to Russian Hybrid Warfare
sub.descr: German officials said the incident is part of a pattern of hybrid warfare, a strategy that involves covert operations, sabotage, cyberattacks and influence campaigns. Berlin has accused Moscow of trying to undermine European support for Ukraine by attacking infrastructure and sowing insecurity among European populations. Germany and other European countries have previously raised the alarm over suspected Russian-linked activities, including espionage, cyber attacks and plots to commit sabotage. The latest allegation has heightened fears that the war between Russia and Ukraine is increasingly spilling beyond the battlefield.

sub.title: Germany Responds With Diplomatic Retaliation
sub.descr: Following the charge Germany has announced measures aimed at Russian diplomatic and cultural institutions. The government announced it would close the Russian consulate in Bonn and the Russian House cultural center in Berlin. Germany has also got other things up their sleeve, including sanctions and security measures. The German officials reportedly summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident. Berlin has also said it will work with European partners to coordinate any further response.

sub.title: Russia Denies German Accusations
sub.descr: Russia has denied any involvement in the drone incident and dismissed Germany's accusations as politically motivated. Moscow has previously dismissed similar accusations from European governments, saying Western countries were using security allegations to justify hostile policies toward Russia. The Kremlin has denied any responsibility for the incident in Leipzig, and questioned the evidence presented by the German authorities.

sub.title: Attack Sparks Security Fears Across Europe
sub.descr: The Leipzig incident has raised concerns over the vulnerability of European infrastructure. European governments are beefing up security at airports, energy facilities, transportation networks and military-related sites as they watch for potential sabotage threats. Officials say Russia has increasingly turned to unconventional tactics as Western countries continue to back Ukraine. Germany's charge is emblematic of growing fears that Russia's confrontation with NATO countries may include activities that stop short of conventional military conflict.

sub.title: Ukraine Link Makes Airport a Strategic Target
sub.descr: Due to its status as a major European logistics hub, Leipzig/Halle Airport is strategically important. The airport has handled large cargo operations, including flights related to Ukrainian transport requirements. German officials are worried this link could have made the site a target. The episode shows how the infrastructure that supports Ukraine has become a security concern for European allies.

sub.title: NATO Allies Await Germany's Response
sub.descr: Germany's response is being closely watched by NATO allies. Officials have insisted on a coordinated European approach to counter suspected hybrid threats. The incident may have repercussions for future discussions on protecting critical infrastructure and building defenses against drone attacks. NATO has expressed support for Germany in the wake of the accusations.

sub.title: The Growing Importance of Drone Warfare
sub.descr: The episode shows how drones have become central not just to the conduct of battles, but to broader security challenges. In the Russia-Ukraine war, drones have been extensively used for surveillance, strikes and disruption of infrastructure. European governments are now throwing money at counter-drone systems to protect airports, military bases and critical facilities. The Leipzig event has added to pressure on governments to boost their detection and response capabilities.

sub.title: Europe's Security Climate
sub.descr: The German charge comes as European nations re-evaluate their security strategies after years of growing tensions with Russia. European governments have changed their view on threats to civilian infrastructure since the war in Ukraine. Officials warn future conflicts could involve a combination of military operations, cyberattacks, misinformation campaigns and covert sabotage.

sub.title: What Comes Next
sub.descr: Germany is likely to continue working diplomatically with its European allies but will boost security around critical infrastructure. The charge against Russia could bring about more sanctions or joint European government action. Moscow's rejection of the accusations is likely to add to the strain in relations between Berlin and Moscow. The Leipzig airport drone incident has become a major test of Europe's response to suspected hybrid warfare and Germany has warned that protecting critical infrastructure is now a central security priority.

title: Herzog Gives Eisenkot First Shot at Forming Government
shortdescription: President Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form Israel's next government, but he faces tough coalition choices and a tight six-week window.

sub.title: Herzog Gives Eisenkot the First Shot at Forming a Government
sub.descr:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog formally gave opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form the country's next government on Sunday evening. The step is a milestone for the former military chief, who is trying to end the long run in power of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader.

It does not make Eisenkot prime minister. He now has up to six weeks to assemble a coalition, which will be hard because the October 27 election left neither his bloc nor Netanyahu's with a clear majority in the Knesset. Herzog said that in his consultations with the parties, a majority of lawmakers backed giving Eisenkot the task.

At the ceremony at the presidential residence in Jerusalem, Herzog said he hoped that whatever government emerges would bring unity, connection and healing, adding that the country has only one home. Eisenkot promised leadership that the public can trust and that represents every part of society. He said an absolute majority of Knesset members support change, and that he would proceed with patience, humility and composure.

sub.title: Arab-Led Parties Could Decide the Outcome
sub.descr:
Among the possible kingmakers, and the most politically sensitive allies, are the Arab-led parties, which made historic gains after high turnout among Israel's Arab citizens. Only one Arab party, Ra'am, has ever joined a governing coalition, back in 2021. Ra'am says it will back Eisenkot, but it doesn't have enough seats to give him a majority by itself.

The other Arab-led party, the Joint List, broke with decades of precedent by offering to support him from outside the coalition to end Netanyahu's hold on power. That would be uncomfortable for both sides. The Joint List would be backing a government that is unlikely to end Israel's wars or slow settlement growth in the occupied West Bank. Eisenkot and his allies would be aligning with parties that reject Israel's identity as a Jewish state.

sub.title: Conditions, Conflicts and Claims of a Stolen Vote
sub.descr:
One of his partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beytenu, has already said it won't sit in a coalition with Arab-led parties. Eisenkot has set four conditions for anyone who wants to join: recognize Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept its declaration of independence, support military, national or civil service for all citizens, and label Hamas a terrorist group. It's unclear whether the Arab parties will accept them.

Netanyahu, meanwhile, has repeatedly made unproven claims that Arab parties stole the election, and he argues that any alliance with them would be a betrayal. The Shin Bet has opened a probe into possible foreign interference, but the Central Elections Committee and Herzog say the vote was valid and that any wrongdoing found would not have changed the outcome significantly.

sub.title: Hard Choices on the Road to a Majority
sub.descr:
Eisenkot says he wants to form a government as quickly as possible, but each likely path seems to involve compromises or broken promises. Besides seeking Arab-party support, he has two other options: a power-sharing deal with Netanyahu, or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties.

The second option is awkward. Equal military service was a central part of the campaign run by Eisenkot and his partners, and they want to end the long-standing draft exemptions. The religious parties, who were in Netanyahu's outgoing coalition, want to keep them, calling them essential to a devout way of life. The exemptions have become more controversial with the public after three years of war.

sub.title: What Happens If Eisenkot Cannot Form a Government
sub.descr:
United Torah Judaism, aware that it could be a swing vote, has left the door open to working with Eisenkot. He has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible two-week extension from the president. If he fails, Netanyahu could be given a turn, and if both fail, Israel would go back to elections early next spring.

New members of the Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday evening. Until a coalition is in place, Netanyahu and his cabinet stay on in a caretaker role with limited powers.

sub.title: Wars and Shifting Support Abroad Await the Next Government
sub.descr:
The next government will inherit heavy burdens. Despite fragile ceasefires, Israel's military is still fighting Hamas in Gaza and Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, and the war Israel launched jointly with the United States against Iran is unresolved.

Both Herzog and Eisenkot mentioned those challenges, along with what Herzog called the new political situation in the United States, where the midterm elections suggested weaker support for Israel across party lines.

sub.title: Trump and Herzog Weigh In on the Contest
sub.descr:
Asked about Eisenkot getting the first chance, President Donald Trump said Netanyahu and Eisenkot have very similar views and are both strong on what he does. He said it's a contest between the two and that we'll see what happens.

Herzog closed by urging Eisenkot to use his military leadership and his own experience of loss, since Eisenkot lost a son in combat in Gaza, to unite the country. He reminded him that as the negotiations begin, the whole nation, with its pain, hopes and fears, is watching.
